findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new code added to getClient() calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (unlike every other service in this PR). Any use of the Salesforce calendar service will throw a ReferenceError/TS compile error as soon as the token refresh path runs, breaking Salesforce event creation and updates entirely.

findings.title: Sync-mode return type is a fetch Response but callers expect provider SDK results (.data, parsed JSON)
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw `fetch` Response of the sync endpoint. However the wrapped call sites were written for provider-specific return shapes: Google's CalendarService does `const token = res?.data; ... token.access_token` (googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 94), Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin do `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data` (zohocrm line 217, zoho-bigin line 96). A fetch Response has no `.data` property, so in sync mode these call sites will read `undefined` and crash with a TypeError (or silently corrupt behavior) instead of refreshing tokens. The abstraction needs a normalized return type (e.g. always parsed JSON or always a Response-like with `.data`).

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted
findings.body: When the (sync-mode) token response lacks a refresh_token, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Consumers then persist this value to the credential row: Zoom (VideoApiAdapter line 120-124 `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`) and Webex (lines 101-107) both write the stored key back to the DB. This overwrites the user's real refresh token with a garbage placeholder, permanently bricking the integration once the access token expires, since future refreshes will send the literal string "refresh_token" as the grant.

findings.title: Computed zod keys do not implement "any numeric property is the expiry"
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create catch-all/optional keys in a zod object. The computed key evaluates to a literal string like "[ZodString]", so the schema actually only requires `access_token`, and unknown keys are stripped by default. The intent (accept any numeric property as expiry, allow other properties through) is not achieved, and since zod strips unknown keys, any expiry field returned by the sync endpoint (e.g. `expiry_date`, `expires_in`) is silently dropped from `data` — callers like Google (`token.expiry_date`) then read undefined and write `expiry_date: undefined` into the credential key.

findings.title: credentialId passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: The third argument of refreshOAuthTokens is the Cal.com user id (used as `calcomUserId` in the sync request), but zoho-bigin passes `credentialId` (the credential row id) instead of `credential.userId`. In sync mode the parent application will receive the wrong identifier and refresh the wrong (or no) user's tokens, breaking Bigin token refresh for every user.

findings.title: No HTTP method check and unhandled zod/JSON.parse errors return 500s
findings.body: The handler does not verify `req.method === "POST"`, so GET/PUT etc. reach the body parsing. Additionally `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (line 57) throw on invalid input; Next's default error handling will surface these as unstyled 500 errors instead of a 400 with a meaningful message, unlike the rest of the handler which carefully returns 403/404 JSON. A malformed or non-JSON request crashes instead of being rejected cleanly.

findings.title: Token endpoint now hit on every Salesforce service instantiation
findings.body: Previously jsforce refreshed tokens lazily via its own connection logic. The new getClient() unconditionally POSTs to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token and writes the credential row on every construction of SalesforceCalendarService (constructor awaits getClient). This means every booking operation involving Salesforce now performs an extra network round-trip and a DB write per request, even when the stored access token is still valid — a performance regression and unnecessary token churn for non-sync deployments.

findings.title: Sync-mode refresh response is fed to handleLarkError which expects Lark's envelope format
findings.body: In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's response, but the code then runs `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, ...)` (line 84) which expects Lark's `{code: 0, data: {...}}` envelope, and builds new credentials from `data.data.refresh_token` / `data.data.refresh_expires_in`. Unless the self-hoster's endpoint happens to mimic Lark's exact envelope (undocumented), the refresh fails or produces undefined fields in the persisted key. The expected response contract for the sync endpoint is never defined and differs per app, making this integration unusable as written.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with plain !== (non-constant-time) and header value may be an array
findings.body: The secret check uses `!==` on `req.headers[...]`, which is a timing-observable comparison and, since Node header lookup can return string[] for repeated headers, a duplicate header could make the comparison fail unpredictably (or bypass intent if arrays are coerced). Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual) on a string-coerced header, as done for other webhook secrets in the codebase.

findings.title: Sync request carries no authentication to the credential sync endpoint
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no auth header/signature, so any party that can reach the endpoint can request fresh OAuth tokens for arbitrary users. Since this endpoint hands out third-party access tokens, the request should be authenticated (e.g. with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) and ideally use HTTPS — neither is enforced or documented.

findings.title: Redirect URI change is unrelated and diverges from callback path derivation
findings.body: The redirect URI was changed from the dynamic `` `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback` `` to the hardcoded `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback`. If appConfig.slug is ever renamed or the app is mounted under a different slug, add.ts and callback.ts (which still uses `${appConfig.slug}/callback` at line 36) will produce mismatched redirect URIs and Zoho will reject the token exchange. At minimum both files should derive the path the same way; ideally drop this unrelated drive-by change.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: The export evaluates to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which yields the string value of the encryption key (not `true`) when both are set. Any consumer doing strict equality (`=== true`) or serializing/inspecting this flag will behave unexpectedly; export `!!(...)` instead.
